newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Slower growth seen in UK Feb retail sales.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Slower growth seen in UK Feb retail sales.

text.p: Activity on Britain's high streets is expected to have slowed in February as a long spell of wet weather kept retail sales volumes relatively tame, economists said.
But the scene will not remain subdued for long, with new-found consumer spending power likely to filter through to retailers later on this year.
February retail sales, due at 0930 GMT on Wednesday, will slow to a seasonally-adjusted rise of 0.1 percent on the month, from 0.6 percent gain in January, according to a Reuter poll.
The annual rate is forecast to have fallen to 3.6 percent from 4.6 percent in January, although analysts said some of this sharp decline would be due to strong sales figures in February 1996.
"All the signs suggest that the pace of high street activity slowed further in February," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets in London.
She cited the latest Confederation of British Industry (CBI) distributive trades survey, which showed the reported sales balance falling to its lowest level since November 1995.
The CBI survey also showed a fall in the price expectations balance, David said, suggesting retailers would remain reticent about trying to top up margins.
"Retailers are not confident of being able to raise prices without being punished by price-conscious consumers over the next few months -- which bodes well for the inflation outlook."
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, also said recent survey evidence suggested retailers -- particularly in the footwear sector -- were seeing a slowing trend in sales volumes.
But, forecasting an unchanged growth rate in February from January and a year-on-year rate of 3.5 percent, Barr said the underlying trend remained robust.

Philip Shaw, economist at Union Plc, agreed high street activity was unlikely to stay down for long. While he expects a fall in year-on-year retail sales to 3.2 percent in February, he said the retrenchment in growth was likely to prove temporary.
"Over the remainder of 1997, a continued improvement in personal incomes is likely to push consumer spending growth up further," Shaw said.
But while sales would resume their upward path further out, there was little danger of a return to the "uncontrolled boom" of the mid-1980s.
